frontmatter_description: Diagnose how a character weights competing goals when more than one desire is active.
title: Goal-Conflict Arbitration
use_when: Use when the question asks which of two or more active goals matters more to the character.
Use when the task is to identify the weighting rule behind a choice among competing wants, motives, or aims.
Use when the scene does not depend on a prior commitment, fixed schedule, or explicit obligation.
do_not_use_when: Do not use when the question is really about the next action the character will take; use action prediction instead.
Do not use when an existing commitment, ongoing plan, or invitation sets the priority; use commitment priority instead.
Do not use when the issue is emotion from success, loss, threat, or blame; use an emotion-appraisal skill instead.
Do not use when the question is about intention recognition, persuasion, or social meaning rather than goal weighting.
decision_variable: which goal gets greater weight in the character's prioritization rule
trigger_checklist: Two or more goals are active at the same time.
The question asks which goal wins, outweighs, or dominates.
No fixed commitment already settles the choice.
The answer depends on priority, salience, urgency, reward, cost, or value tradeoff.
workflow: Identify all competing goals that are active in the scene.
Check what the question asks to compare: priority, strength, urgency, payoff, or moral cost.
Infer the weighting rule the character is using.
Choose the goal that the rule makes dominant.

special_case.title: Tie or near-tie between goals
special_case.rule: If the scene gives no commitment and no explicit priority cue, use the strongest stated incentive, threat, or immediate payoff to break the tie.

worked_example.scene: Dana wants to leave early to meet a friend, but also wants to finish a task before the meeting.
worked_example.question: Which goal wins?
worked_example.answer_logic: Compare the active goals and look for the stronger stated weight. If the task has a deadline or major cost, it outweighs the meeting; if not, the social plan may win. The key variable is the weighting rule, not the exact action sequence.

boundary_exit_rule: Exit immediately to micro-23 Action Prediction if the question asks what the character will do next rather than how goals are weighted.
Exit immediately to micro-24 Commitment Priority if an existing obligation, plan, or invitation determines the answer.
Exit immediately to micro-21 Goal Hierarchy if the question asks how local goals nest under broader goals rather than which one outweighs the other.
Exit immediately to an emotion-appraisal unit (micro-26 to micro-31) if the scene is about how the character feels about gain, loss, threat, blame, or success.
Exit immediately to micro-22 or a belief unit if the scene is about intention reading or belief inference without active goal competition.

references.route_signal: Use this micro unit when the answer depends on how a character compares competing goals, not on a fixed commitment or a predicted next move.
hard_boundary: Goal-Conflict Arbitration weights two active wants; if a binding promise or schedule pre-resolves the choice, route to micro-24 Commitment Priority.
It outputs which goal is weighted higher, not the next observable behavior; behavioral output is micro-23 Action Prediction.
It is about goal weighting at the desire level, not feeling about the outcome; emotion is micro-26 to micro-31.
It treats goals as parallel competitors, not as nested means-and-ends; nesting is micro-21 Goal Hierarchy.
shortcut_to_avoid: Do not infer the most visible action and treat it as the whole goal structure.
Do not assume a schedule or obligation unless the scene explicitly gives one.
Do not convert a motivation question into an emotion question.
common_failure_modes: Confusing goal weighting with next-step prediction.
Using commitment priority when the scene only shows general desire conflict.
Reading emotion as if it were the main cause of the choice.
Answering with personality labels instead of the active weighting rule.

minimal_pair.case: A character wants to study and also wants to go to a party, with no deadline or promise involved.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: This is direct competition between goals, so the task is to infer which goal gets more weight.

minimal_pair.case: A character promised to help a friend but now also wants to rest.
minimal_pair.why_it_matches: This looks similar, but the promise introduces commitment priority, which is outside this unit.

boundary_stress_test: If removing the commitment would change the answer, this is not Goal-Conflict Arbitration.
If the question can be answered by naming the next action alone, it belongs elsewhere.
If the key clue is an emotion word rather than a goal tradeoff, leave this unit.
references.generalization_note: This unit covers general goal tradeoffs across everyday, moral, social, and self-protective motives, as long as no prior commitment resolves the choice.

validation_seed.positive_pattern: The character faces two active goals and the answer depends on which goal is weighted more strongly.
validation_seed.near_miss_pattern: The character has two goals, but one is already governed by a promise, schedule, or standing obligation.
validation_seed.boundary_pattern: The question asks what the character will do next, not how the character ranks the goals.

notes: Keep the unit focused on goal weighting, not full planning.
Use only when the scene lacks a prior commitment that settles the conflict.
This micro skill should support diagnosis inside broader goal-and-action routes.
core_question: Determine how a character chooses among conflicting goals
